stem: Powders P and Q both look white. In 100 mL of water under the same conditions, 2 g of P dissolves and 18 g of Q dissolves. Which evidence tells P and Q apart, and why is color not enough?
answer: Solubility tells them apart: P dissolves 2 g and Q dissolves 18 g in 100 mL of water. Both look white, so color alone cannot tell them apart.
steps: names the solubility record (2 g against 18 g) as the evidence | says the powders share a color, so color cannot separate them
samples: Solubility: P dissolves 2 g and Q dissolves 18 g, so they differ even though both are white. Color alone cannot tell them apart. | Color tells them apart, or: they are both white so they are the same substance.

stem: Two liquids are mixed and a solid is separated out. The solid has measured properties (density, melting point, how well it dissolves) that differ from both liquids. What evidence supports a new substance rather than only a mixture?
answer: The separated solid has a property profile that differs from both liquids, so it is a different substance. Mixing alone does not show a new substance.
steps: points to the separated solid having properties that differ from both liquids | says mixing alone is not enough to show a new substance
samples: The solid's measured properties differ from both liquids, so it is a new substance. Just mixing two liquids would not show that. | Any time two things are mixed you get a new substance.

stem: Group sheet. Under What we saw, list what you observed and what the scale read. Under What we think is happening, write your group's explanation for the gas. After the safety sheet, write one safety rule from today and what it protects.
answer: What we saw holds only observations and readings (bubbles rising, the solid getting smaller until gone, the scale reading before and after). What we think is happening holds an explanation for the gas. One safety rule is named with the harm it prevents.
steps: What we saw holds observations or readings only, with no explanation in it | What we think is happening holds at least one explanation for the gas | one safety rule is named and what it protects is said
samples: What we saw: bubbles rose, the solid got smaller until it was gone, the scale read lower after. What we think: the gas formed when the powders met the water. Rule: goggles on, to keep powder and splashes out of eyes. | What we saw: the powder made a gas from the water. Rule: be careful.

stem: A classmate says chalk in vinegar "vanished." Drawing 1: no particles are left in the open cup. Drawing 2: some leave through the top. (a) Which drawing agrees with her, and what does the other show? (b) Write a question a mass reading could answer, and what a lower reading shows.
answer: (a) Drawing 1 agrees with the classmate, since no particles are left in the cup; drawing 2 shows the matter did not vanish: some of it left the cup through the open top. (b) For example: Did anything leave the cup? A lower reading means something left the cup.
steps: (a) picks drawing 1 as the one that agrees with the claim and says drawing 2 shows the matter did not vanish, some of it left through the top | (b) asks a question a mass reading can answer | (b) says a lower reading means something left the cup, not that matter is gone
samples: (a) Drawing 1 agrees with her; drawing 2 shows the matter is not gone, some of it left through the top. (b) Did anything leave the cup? If the reading is lower, something left the cup. | (a) They are different drawings. (b) What is the gas called? A lower reading means the matter is gone.

stem: A student drops a seltzer tablet in water and says, "The gas comes from the water, not the tablet." (a) Name a test that could count against her claim, and the result that would. (b) Before a teacher-only demonstration, a classmate's long hair hangs loose beside the tray. Say one thing to do.
answer: (a) Any fair test with a result named, for example: put the same amount of plain water in a matching cup and watch. If the water alone made the gas, it would bubble too; no bubbles counts against her claim. (b) Say to tie the hair back before anything is opened.
steps: (a) names a test that could count against the claim | (a) names the result that would count against it | (b) says to tie the hair back before anything is opened
samples: (a) Put plain water in a matching cup and watch it. If it does not bubble, that counts against her claim. (b) Say tie your hair back before the powder comes out. | (a) Bubbles show a reaction, so her claim is proved. (b) Be careful.

stem: A dish of water sits on a sunny windowsill and is dry the next day. A student writes: Claim, the water stopped existing. Evidence, I cannot see it any more. (a) Which part does the evidence fail to support? (b) Name a second piece of evidence.
answer: (a) Not seeing the water shows only that it is hidden or has moved; it does not show the water stopped existing. (b) For example: cover the dish with a clear lid and look for drops collecting on the lid, or seal a dish of water and read it before and after: the reading stays the same.
steps: (a) says the evidence fails to support the claim that it stopped existing | (a) says not seeing it shows only that it is hidden or moved | (b) names a second piece of evidence that could be observed or measured
samples: (a) Not seeing it only shows it is hidden or moved, not that it stopped existing. (b) Cover the dish with a clear lid and look for drops on the lid. | (a) The evidence is enough: it dried up, so it is gone. (b) Look at it again.

stem: A puffed flexible pouch of yeast, sugar and warm water reads 61.2 g before and 61.2 g after. A student says, "The reading did not change, so gas weighs nothing." She opens it and lets the gas out. It reads 60.8 g. Is her claim supported? How many grams left, and what does that show?
answer: Not supported. The gas was still inside the boundary, so the closed reading stayed 61.2 g. When it was let out the reading fell by 0.4 g, which is gas leaving, so gas has mass.
steps: says the claim is not supported | says the gas was still inside the boundary in the closed reading | finds 0.4 g left and says it shows gas has mass
samples: Not supported. The gas was still inside the pouch, so the reading stayed 61.2 g. After it was let out the reading fell 0.4 g, so gas has mass. | Supported: equal readings show gas has no mass.

stem: A vessel sends gas by a leaky tube to a collector. Vessel: 132.8 g before, 132.0 g after. Collector: 44.5 g before, 45.1 g after. (a) How many grams left the vessel, reached the collector, and are in neither? Where could they be? (b) Can these readings tell you which gas it is? Write yes or no and why.
answer: (a) 0.8 g left the vessel and 0.6 g reached the collector, so 0.2 g are in neither: they crossed a boundary into the air through the leak. (b) No. Mass shows only that matter crossed a boundary; it does not name the gas.

stem: A laboratory model represents rain on stone. P is the stone mineral and Q a rain ingredient. After they interact, a solid R is recovered. These profiles are invented for practice and name no real substances. Densities and solubilities are at 20 degrees Celsius; melting and boiling points are at one atmosphere. Density, grams per milliliter: P 2.4, Q 1.1, R 1.7. Melting point, degrees Celsius: P 730, Q -12, R 84. Boiling point, degrees Celsius: P 1,450, Q 112, R 260. Solubility, grams in 100 milliliters of water: P 0.2, Q 40, R 12. Burns: P no, Q no, R no. Odor: P, Q and R are all odorless. Compare every property of R with P and Q, decide whether a reaction took place, and justify your decision.
answer: R differs from both P and Q in density (1.7 against 2.4 and 1.1), melting point (84 against 730 and -12), boiling point (260 against 1,450 and 112) and solubility (12 against 0.2 and 40). All three do not burn and are odorless, so those two properties match. The four differences support a reaction; two shared properties cannot show R is the same as P or Q. Score 6: half a point for each of 6 accurate comparisons (3), 1 for the supported decision, 2 for explaining why matching odor and flammability do not outweigh four differences.
steps: compares R with P and Q on density, melting point, boiling point and solubility | notes that burning and odor match across all three | decides a reaction took place from the changed property profile | says matching odor and flammability do not outweigh the four differences
samples: R's density 1.7 differs from P's 2.4 and Q's 1.1; its melting point 84 differs from 730 and -12; its boiling point 260 differs from 1,450 and 112; its solubility 12 differs from 0.2 and 40. All three do not burn and are odorless. The four differences support a reaction; two shared properties cannot establish identity. | The stone broke, so it reacted.

stem: Use the weathering record of item 1. Scraping a dry sample of P gives fragments with the same profile as P. Draw and label how a different arrangement of atoms could account for R's new properties, using X and Y for two kinds of atom, and say this is a hypothetical model. Then use the scraped-P control to explain what crumbling alone does and does not show.
answer: A labeled hypothetical drawing: before P [X-X] and Q [Y-Y]; after R [X-Y] [X-Y]. Changed groupings could explain R's new profile. The scraped P stays [X-X] with unchanged properties, so crumbling alone is a physical change and shows no reaction. Score 4: different arrangements before and after (2), arrangements linked to different bulk properties (1), control explained (1).
steps: shows different arrangements before and after, labeled as hypothetical | links the arrangements to R's different properties | uses the scraped-P control: unchanged properties mean fragmenting only | keeps every atom of X and Y in the drawing
samples: Hypothetical model: before P [X-X] and Q [Y-Y]; after R [X-Y] [X-Y]. X and Y are atom types and a hyphen joins atoms in a group. Changed groupings could explain R's new profile. Scraped P stays [X-X], so unchanged properties show fragmenting, not a reaction. | The product's particles must be unchanged because matter remains.

stem: A paper case, never a classroom procedure. A record shows a peroxide forming water and oxygen gas. One peroxide molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms. One water molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. One oxygen gas molecule has 2 oxygen atoms. Start with 2 peroxide molecules. (a) Draw a before-and-after model, counting each kind of atom. (b) A flexible closed apparatus and its contents read 142.6 g before and 142.6 g after. After the gas is let out through an opening it reads 141.9 g. Use your model and a drawn boundary to explain both readings. The unchanged solvent stays inside the boundary but is not drawn.
answer: Before: 4 hydrogen atoms and 4 oxygen atoms (2 peroxide molecules). After: 2 water molecules and 1 oxygen molecule, still 4 hydrogen atoms and 4 oxygen atoms. The atom counts are unchanged, so the closed apparatus still reads 142.6 g. When the oxygen gas crosses the boundary through the opening, the apparatus reads 0.7 g lower, 141.9 g; no atoms disappear. Score 8: 2 for each of four parts.
steps: shows 4 hydrogen and 4 oxygen atoms to begin with | regroups them into 2 water molecules and 1 oxygen molecule with the counts unchanged | uses conserved atoms to explain the closed reading staying 142.6 g | shows the gas atoms crossing the boundary and explains the 0.7 g lower reading
samples: Braces enclose the apparatus and contents. Before: {H-O-O-H H-O-O-H}. Closed after: {H-O-H H-O-H O-O}. Both have 4 hydrogen and 4 oxygen atoms, so the total mass stays 142.6 g. Open after: {H-O-H H-O-H}, with O-O outside. Water stays inside; oxygen crosses the boundary. The apparatus loses 0.7 g to its surroundings and reads 141.9 g; no atoms disappear. | The missing 0.7 g stopped existing.
